name: UI treatment
controls: How the product interface itself is visually represented inside the motion graphic.
question: How should the product's interface appear on screen?
notes: UI treatment is a stack, not a single label: a typical launch film combines one fidelity level (how close to the real product), one aesthetic (surface language), one framing (what holds the UI), and optionally a construction move or content pattern (e.g. simplified + glassmorphic + deviceless, or stylized + flat + exploded). Pick at most one per family. Fidelity terms (production-faithful, simplified, abstracted, stylized) are studio vocabulary rather than a formal standard; many teams say 'hi-fi / lo-fi' or 'real UI vs. designed UI'. Aesthetic terms with the -morphism suffix (neumorphism, glassmorphism, claymorphism) are Dribbble-era trend names: widely understood, but informal. FUI (fantasy/fictional user interface) is established screen-graphics jargon from film. Use the facets (border, radius, shadow, density, realism, hierarchy, component scale, spacing, role) to pin the surface details that the option labels leave open.

families.name: Fidelity (how close to the real product)
Construction (how the UI is broken apart or scaled)
Content pattern (what kind of interface it is)

options.what: Surfaces separated only by fill contrast, spacing or shadow; no strokes.
options.prompt: Use no strokes on cards, inputs or panels: separate surfaces with a 3-6% luminance step between background and card fill, or with shadow; keep dividers out entirely.

options.what: Sub-pixel or 0.5px strokes that read as a faint edge, typical of Apple and Linear-style dark UI.
options.prompt: Outline every card, input and panel with a 0.5px stroke (1px at 2x device scale) at 6-10% white on dark or 8-12% black on light; no heavier strokes anywhere.

options.what: A standard 1px low-contrast stroke defining components without drawing attention.
options.prompt: Give cards, inputs and panels a 1px solid border at roughly 10-15% contrast against their fill (e.g. #E5E7EB on white, rgba(255,255,255,0.12) on dark); dividers use the same color.

options.what: A clearly visible 2px stroke that structures the layout and reads at video resolution.
options.prompt: Outline components with a 2px solid border at 25-40% contrast or in a brand color; focused or active elements switch to a 2px accent stroke.

options.what: 3-4px near-black strokes used as a primary graphic device, as in neo-brutalist UI.
options.prompt: Outline every component with a 3-4px solid #000 (or ink-color) border, including buttons, inputs, avatars and chart frames; do not soften with opacity.

options.what: A second outline or solid block offset behind the component, giving a printed, layered edge.
options.prompt: Draw each card with a 2px border plus a duplicate outline or solid block offset 4-8px down and right behind it; on press, translate the card onto the offset so the gap closes.

options.what: Square corners on every component: technical, editorial or brutalist.
options.prompt: Set border-radius to 0 on all cards, buttons, inputs, images and chart containers; no rounding anywhere, including avatars unless they are explicitly circular.

options.what: Barely rounded corners that soften without reading as rounded.
options.prompt: Use 2px radius on inputs, tags and small controls and 4px on cards and panels; keep the ratio consistent so nested elements never exceed their parent radius.

options.what: The default contemporary SaaS rounding.
options.prompt: Use 8px radius on buttons and inputs, 12px on cards and panels; nested elements use parent radius minus padding (concentric corners).

options.what: Soft, friendly rounding typical of mobile, bento and consumer UI.
options.prompt: Use 16px radius on buttons and inputs, 20-24px on cards and sheets, and continuous (squircle-like) corners where possible; inner elements stay concentric.

options.what: Radius equal to half the height: capsule buttons, chips and search bars.
options.prompt: Make buttons, chips, search bars, toggles and tags fully rounded (border-radius: 9999px); cards may stay at 20-24px so the pills read as distinct controls.

options.what: Completely flat surfaces; depth only from color and layout.
options.prompt: Use no box-shadows or drop shadows; separate layers only with fill contrast, borders or spacing.

options.what: One large, low-opacity blurred shadow that lifts a surface gently.
options.prompt: Give raised surfaces a single shadow: 0 12px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.08) on light backgrounds, 0 16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,0.4) on dark; no hard edge.

options.what: Stacked contact plus ambient shadows that scale with elevation levels, Material-style.
options.prompt: Use a two-layer shadow per elevation level: level 1 = 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.06), 0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.10); level 3 = 0 4px 6px rgba(0,0,0,0.05), 0 10px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.10); raise the level (not just opacity) on hover and when elements lift during animation.

options.what: An unblurred solid shadow block, the signature of neo-brutalist UI.
options.prompt: Use a 0-blur solid shadow offset 4-6px right and down in #000 or ink color (box-shadow: 5px 5px 0 #000); pressing a control animates the element to translate(5px,5px) and the shadow to 0.

options.what: Shadows inside the surface, making it look pressed or recessed.
options.prompt: Render wells, inputs and pressed states with inset shadows: inset 0 2px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.12) plus an inset 0 -1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,0.6) highlight; pair with a raised state for toggles.

options.what: A colored, zero-offset blurred halo that emits light from an element, common on dark UI.
options.prompt: Give accent elements a zero-offset glow in the accent color: 0 0 24px 0 accent at 35-50% opacity, plus a tighter 0 0 4px at 80%; reserve glow for 1-2 focal elements per frame.

options.what: Few controls, lots of empty space; one or two actions per view.
options.prompt: Show no more than 3-5 interactive elements per screen; controls are 48px+ tall and at least 40% of the frame is empty surface.

options.what: Typical consumer SaaS density: readable, clearly grouped.
options.prompt: Use 36-40px control heights, 8-12 visible controls per screen grouped into 2-4 clear sections, with 16-24px gaps between groups.

options.what: Compact rows, tables and toolbars, as in IDEs, trading or pro tools.
options.prompt: Use 24-28px row and control heights, 12-13px UI text, tight 4-8px gaps, multiple toolbars and data columns; the density itself signals capability, so zoom in to one region for any story beat.

options.what: Real product UI with real copy, data and components.
options.prompt: Use real component styling, real product copy and plausible real data (names, numbers, timestamps); nothing may contradict the shipping product.

options.what: Recognisably software, but redesigned: real structure, invented surface and simplified content.
options.prompt: Keep the real layout structure but restyle surfaces for the film: larger type, placeholder bars for secondary text, brand color emphasis, simplified data.

options.what: UI reduced to signs: rounded rectangles, lines and dots that stand for interface.
options.prompt: Represent interface only as geometric tokens: rounded rectangles for cards, 6-8px gray bars for text lines, circles for avatars, a single accent shape for the key action; no real text except one hero label.

options.what: One element dominates; everything else recedes.
options.prompt: Make one element the only high-contrast, full-opacity, accent-colored item; dim everything else to 30-50% opacity or desaturate it, and let the camera frame that element.

options.what: A clear lead element with a supporting tier.
options.prompt: Give one primary element full contrast and accent color, 2-3 secondary elements at 70-80% contrast, and all remaining UI at 40%; animate in that order.

options.what: All modules carry equal weight, as in grids and bento overviews.
options.prompt: Give every card equal size, contrast and weight; no accent highlighting; the grid rhythm is the message, so animate cards with a uniform 40-60ms stagger.

options.what: UI at its real on-screen proportions relative to the frame.
options.prompt: Show the interface at its native proportions: a full screen fills 70-90% of the frame width, text at real UI sizes relative to that screen.

options.what: UI scaled 1.5-3x so components read clearly in video.
options.prompt: Scale UI 1.5-3x relative to true scale so body text renders at 28px+ in a 1920x1080 frame; crop the screen to the region in use.

options.what: A single component blown up to fill most of the frame as a graphic object.
options.prompt: Scale one component (button, toggle, input) to fill 50-80% of the frame height; keep its real proportions, radius and border ratios so it still reads as that control.

options.what: Compact padding and gaps, 4-8px rhythm.
options.prompt: Use 4px base spacing: 8px card padding, 4-8px gaps between elements, 12px between sections.

options.what: Conventional 8-point spacing system.
options.prompt: Snap every padding, gap and size to multiples of 8px: 16px control padding, 24px card padding, 32-48px section gaps.

options.what: Oversized padding and whitespace for a premium, calm read.
options.prompt: Use 32-48px card padding, 24px+ gaps between elements, 80px+ between sections; let empty surface occupy at least half of every card.

options.what: Reads as working software the viewer could use: legible, causal, with real states.
options.prompt: Every visible control must be legible and behave causally: clicks produce state changes, data updates respond to input, text is readable for at least 1.5 s.

options.what: UI used as texture or graphic pattern; not meant to be read.
options.prompt: Treat UI as texture: tile, blur, crop or repeat interface fragments at low contrast behind the hero content; no legible text required, no causal interaction.

options.what: The actual shipping interface recreated almost exactly, component for component.
options.looks: Real layouts, real design-system components, true copy, realistic data, native typography and icon set; indistinguishable from a screenshot but vector-clean.
options.motion: Native-feeling transitions that match the product's own motion (sheet slides, list inserts, real hover and pressed states); cursor or touch drives the action at believable speed.
options.use: Product demos, tutorials, onboarding, app-store previews, release notes, anything a customer will compare against the real product.
options.conveys: Honesty and credibility: this is exactly what you get.
options.vs: A screen recording captures the real app with its jank and data; production-faithful UI rebuilds it as clean vectors or HTML so it can be animated freely. Simplified UI starts from the same source but removes detail.
options.prompt: Rebuild the product interface exactly: use the real layout grid, design-system components, fonts, icon set, colors and copy; populate with plausible real data; animate only with state changes the real product actually has, at the product's own transition timings.

options.what: The real interface with non-essential detail removed.
options.looks: Real layout and hierarchy kept; secondary controls, dense tables, nav clutter and placeholder copy stripped or replaced with gray bars; generous spacing; key elements slightly enlarged.
options.motion: Clean UI transitions: panels slide and resize, cursor-led focus, content swaps inside stable frames; the camera pushes in to the region in use.
options.use: SaaS launch films, feature reveals, landing-page heroes.
options.conveys: Clarity and confidence; the product feels easy.
options.vs: Production-faithful keeps everything; simplified keeps the whole screen but cleaner; abstracted keeps only the one or two controls that matter; stylized redesigns the surfaces too.
options.prompt: Represent the product UI as a simplified version of the real interface: keep its true layout, hierarchy and brand components; remove secondary controls, dense data and navigation clutter; replace non-story text with 6-8px gray placeholder bars; enlarge the elements that carry the story 1.2-1.5x.

options.what: Only the controls essential to the story remain; the rest of the interface disappears.
options.looks: One input, one button, one result card floating in space or on a plain surface; recognisable component styling but no surrounding app shell.
options.motion: Focused cause-and-effect: the essential control acts, the result appears; elements morph between states rather than navigating screens.
options.use: Feature highlights, social cut-downs, hero loops, explaining one idea per shot.
options.conveys: Focus and simplicity: the feature is the whole point.
options.vs: Simplified keeps the full screen; abstracted removes the shell entirely. Isolated-component UI is the extreme case (exactly one element); symbolic realism replaces components with geometry.
options.prompt: Strip the interface down to only the 1-3 components the story needs (e.g. the prompt field, the generate button, the output card); remove the app shell, nav and sidebars; keep the real component styling, and animate them morphing between states on a plain background.

options.what: An interface that follows the product's concept but is redesigned for visual impact rather than accuracy.
options.looks: Larger type, exaggerated contrast, brand gradients, idealised data, extra depth or glow; it looks better than the real app and could not ship as-is.
options.motion: Showier than the product: dramatic reveals, 3D tilts, parallax layers, choreographed builds.
options.use: Brand-led launch films, keynote moments, ads, early-stage products with unfinished UI.
options.conveys: Ambition and energy; sells the idea and the feeling over the details.
options.vs: Simplified removes detail but keeps real styling; stylized changes the styling. Illustrative UI goes further and stops looking like software at all.
options.prompt: Redesign the interface for the film while keeping the product's structure recognisable: increase type sizes 1.5x, push contrast, use brand color and gradients on key surfaces, idealise the data (clean round numbers, perfect curves), and add depth (soft shadows, subtle glow) that the real product does not have.

options.what: Interface drawn as an illustration rather than rendered as software.
options.looks: Simplified shapes with illustration line weights and palettes, possibly outlines, textures or characters interacting with oversized screens; text becomes squiggles or bars.
options.motion: Illustration-style animation: squash-and-stretch, drawn-on lines, character interaction, looser timing.
options.use: Explainers, onboarding, marketing sites with an illustration system, brand campaigns.
options.conveys: Warmth and approachability; the product as a friendly concept.
options.vs: Stylized UI still looks like software; illustrative UI looks like a drawing of software. Hand-drawn UI is a specific illustrative aesthetic with imperfect strokes.
options.prompt: Draw the interface as part of an illustration: 2-3px uniform outlines, the illustration palette rather than the product palette, text as rounded gray bars, icons simplified to basic shapes; animate with squash-and-stretch and draw-on strokes rather than UI transitions.

options.what: A low-fidelity representation showing structure only: boxes, lines and placeholder content.
options.looks: Gray or monochrome outlined boxes, X-crossed image placeholders, bar-lines for text, no color or imagery.
options.motion: Build-up animation: boxes draw on, snap into grid positions, then often transition into the finished UI.
options.use: Design-process stories, before/after, design-tool marketing, explaining information architecture.
options.conveys: Process, planning, structure before polish.
options.vs: Skeleton UI is the loading-state placeholder within finished UI (filled gray blocks); wireframe is the design-stage drawing (outlined boxes). Blueprint UI exposes measurements and construction.
options.prompt: Render the interface as a wireframe: 1-1.5px gray (#9CA3AF) outlines on white or near-black, image placeholders as boxes with diagonal crosses, text as 6px rounded bars, no color and no shadows; draw strokes on with a 300-500ms stroke-dashoffset animation and snap boxes into a visible grid.

options.what: Finished-style interface where content is represented by filled neutral placeholder blocks.
options.looks: Real card shapes, radii and spacing, but text lines, avatars and images are solid light-gray blocks, often with a shimmer sweep.
options.motion: Shimmer gradient sweeps left to right; blocks resolve into real content with a crossfade or staggered fill.
options.use: Generic product scenes where content must stay neutral, AI generation (content arriving), loading moments, templates.
options.conveys: Structure and anticipation; content is on its way.
options.vs: Wireframes are outlined design sketches; skeleton UI is styled, filled placeholder inside otherwise polished UI. Symbolic realism is similar but not tied to a loading metaphor.
options.prompt: Build the interface with real card shapes, radii and spacing, but render all content as solid placeholder blocks (#E5E7EB on light, #1F2937 on dark): text lines 8-10px tall at 60-90% widths, circles for avatars; sweep a 30-degree highlight gradient across every 1.2-1.6s, then resolve blocks into real content with a 40ms stagger.

options.what: Interface with its construction intentionally exposed: grids, measurements, guides and annotations.
options.looks: Visible layout grids, redline dimension labels, spacing callouts, bounding boxes, monospace annotation text; often blue or dark ground with thin light lines.
options.motion: Precise, drafting-like: guides extend, dimensions tick in, bounding boxes snap, components assemble on the grid.
options.use: Design-system launches, developer tools, design-tool marketing, technical explainers.
options.conveys: Precision, craft, engineering rigor.
options.vs: Wireframes show structure without measurement; blueprint UI shows how the structure is built (dimensions, spacing, grids). Exploded UI separates layers in depth; blueprint annotates in plane.
options.prompt: Expose the interface's construction: overlay a 12-column grid and 8px baseline in 1px lines at 15% opacity, draw bounding boxes and red or cyan dimension labels (e.g. '24', '8px') in 11px monospace, extend guides with linear 200ms wipes, then snap components into place on the grid.

options.what: Interface rendered with imperfect strokes, doodle shapes and irregular borders.
options.looks: Wobbly marker or pencil outlines, slightly uneven boxes, handwritten labels, hatched fills, paper texture.
options.motion: Boiling lines (stroke jitter every 2-3 frames), draw-on strokes, stop-motion stepping at 12fps.
options.use: Whiteboard explainers, early-stage ideas, playful brands, design-process stories.
options.conveys: Informality, creativity, work-in-progress honesty.
options.vs: Wireframes are clean and mechanical; hand-drawn UI is deliberately imperfect. Illustrative UI can be polished; hand-drawn always shows the hand.
options.prompt: Draw the interface with imperfect 2-3px marker strokes: corners slightly overshoot, lines wobble 1-2px, labels in a handwriting font; animate lines boiling (redraw with new jitter every 2-3 frames at 12fps) and draw strokes on as if sketched live.

options.what: Large empty areas, restrained controls and simple geometry.
options.looks: Monochrome or one-accent palette, few elements, large type, thin or no borders, 50%+ empty surface.
options.motion: Slow, precise, restrained: soft eases, small distances, one move at a time.
options.use: Premium SaaS, productivity tools, Apple-style keynotes, brand films that prize calm.
options.conveys: Calm, focus, confidence, premium quality.
options.vs: Flat UI is about no simulated depth; minimal UI is about reduction and space (it may have soft shadows). Abstracted UI removes the shell; minimal UI can keep it, just sparse.
options.prompt: Design the interface with extreme restraint: one neutral palette plus a single accent, no more than 5 elements per view, 50% or more empty surface, hairline or no borders, one type family in two weights; move one element at a time with long soft eases (power2/power3, 600-900ms).

options.what: Interface with no simulated physical depth: solid fills, no gradients, shadows or textures.
options.looks: Solid color blocks, crisp edges, simple icons, bold contrasting colors; depth only by layout and color.
options.motion: 2D motion only: slides, scales, color fills, wipes; no z-depth or lighting changes.
options.use: Explainers, consumer apps, infographics, brand systems with strong color.
options.conveys: Clarity, modernity, directness.
options.vs: Material UI is flat color plus elevation shadows; flat UI has no shadows at all. Minimal UI is about reduction, flat UI is about the absence of depth cues; they often combine.
options.prompt: Render every UI surface in solid flat color: no gradients, no shadows, no textures, no blur; separate layers by hue and value contrast only; animate strictly in 2D (translate, scale, color change, mask wipes).

options.what: Layered paper-like surfaces with consistent elevation shadows and depth cues.
options.looks: Opaque surfaces stacked at defined elevations, layered shadows growing with height, ripples, floating action buttons.
options.motion: Surfaces lift (shadow grows) on interaction, touch ripples expand from the contact point, shared-element container transforms between screens.
options.use: Android apps, Google products, enterprise dashboards.
options.conveys: Order, tactility, systematic logic.
options.vs: Flat UI has no shadows; skeuomorphic UI imitates specific real materials; Material uses abstract paper-and-ink elevation. Google's Material 3 relies more on tonal color than shadow, so 'Material-style' often means the 2014-era elevation look.
options.prompt: Build UI from opaque surfaces at defined elevation levels (0, 1, 3, 6, 8) with layered contact-plus-ambient shadows; on press, spawn a circular ripple from the touch point expanding over 300ms at 12% opacity, and raise the pressed surface one elevation level; use container-transform transitions between screens.

options.what: Digital objects that imitate physical objects and materials.
options.looks: Leather, felt, wood, brushed metal, stitched edges, realistic knobs and dials, paper notebooks, glossy highlights.
options.motion: Physical-object behavior: knobs rotate, pages curl, switches throw with mechanical snap, needles swing with inertia.
options.use: Nostalgic or retro pieces, audio and music tools, playful brands, parody of pre-2013 UI.
options.conveys: Familiarity, tactility, nostalgia, craftsmanship.
options.vs: Neo-skeuomorphic (soft UI) imitates generic extruded plastic in one color, not specific real materials. Claymorphic imitates inflated clay; skeuomorphic imitates the actual object (a real notepad, a real VU meter).
refs: iOS 6 and earlier (Notes, Game Center, Find My Friends)
options.prompt: Render interface objects as realistic physical materials: textured surfaces (leather, brushed aluminum, paper), bevelled edges with top highlights, realistic knobs and toggles with cast shadows; animate with physical behavior (rotation with inertia, mechanical snap on switches, 150ms settle).

options.what: Monochrome surfaces where controls appear extruded from or pressed into the background using paired light and dark shadows.
options.looks: Background and control share one color; each element has a light shadow top-left and dark shadow bottom-right (or inset for pressed); very low contrast.
options.motion: Controls press in (shadows flip from outset to inset) and pop out; slow, soft transitions.
options.use: Concept pieces, smart-home and device controls, audio apps, trend-driven social content.
options.conveys: Softness, tactility, calm; can read as dated or low-accessibility.
options.vs: Skeuomorphic imitates specific real materials; neumorphism imitates one generic soft plastic surface. Claymorphism uses colored, inflated objects floating over a background, not same-color extrusions. Term popularised on Dribbble around 2019-2020; informal.
options.prompt: Use one background color (e.g. #E0E5EC) for both surface and controls; raise each control with dual shadows (-8px -8px 16px rgba(255,255,255,0.8), 8px 8px 16px rgba(163,177,198,0.6)); pressed states flip to the same values as inset shadows over 200ms; keep radii 16-24px and add a single accent color only for active state.

options.what: Translucent panels that blur what is behind them, like frosted glass.
options.looks: Semi-transparent white or tinted panels with background blur, a thin light border, colorful gradient or photo backdrop showing through.
options.motion: Panels slide over moving color fields; the blurred backdrop shifts as panels move; specular edge highlights catch light.
options.use: OS-style interfaces, premium consumer apps, spatial and visionOS-style pieces, launch films on dark gradients.
options.conveys: Lightness, depth, modernity, layered context.
options.vs: Glass needs something colorful behind it to read; on a flat background it is just a translucent card. Neumorphism is opaque; claymorphism is solid and inflated.
options.prompt: Render panels as frosted glass: background rgba(255,255,255,0.08-0.15), backdrop-filter blur(20-40px) saturate(1.4), a 1px rgba(255,255,255,0.2) border, 20-24px radius; place a slowly drifting colorful gradient or blurred shapes behind so the blur visibly reveals it.

options.what: Soft, inflated, 3D-like components that look moulded from clay or soft plastic.
options.looks: Pastel colored rounded objects with large radii, inner highlights top-left, inner shadows bottom-right and a soft outer drop shadow; toy-like 3D icons.
options.motion: Squashy, bouncy motion: elements squash on press, wobble on settle, float gently.
options.use: Consumer apps, fintech for young audiences, education, playful product marketing.
options.conveys: Friendliness, playfulness, safety.
options.vs: Neumorphism uses same-color extrusions from the background; claymorphism uses colored free-floating objects with inner shading. Informal trend term (circa 2021).
options.prompt: Render components as inflated clay: pastel fills, 24-32px radii, inner highlight (inset 6px 6px 12px rgba(255,255,255,0.6)), inner shadow (inset -6px -6px 12px rgba(0,0,0,0.12)) and a soft outer drop shadow (0 16px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.12)); animate presses with 8-12% squash and a soft elastic settle.

options.what: Heavy black borders, bold type, hard offset shadows and intentionally raw composition.
options.looks: 3-4px black outlines, solid saturated fills (yellow, pink, lime), hard 0-blur shadows, chunky grotesk or mono type, visible grid, little rounding.
options.motion: Snappy and mechanical: instant snaps, hard press offsets (element slides onto its shadow), stepped or linear moves, no soft fades.
options.use: Indie tools, creator economy products, dev tools with personality, bold social content.
options.conveys: Directness, confidence, anti-corporate personality.
options.vs: Architectural brutalism and 2010s web brutalism (raw HTML, default styles) are related but different; neo-brutalist UI is polished rawness with color and hard shadows. Flat UI has no borders or shadows.
options.prompt: Use 3px solid #000 borders on every component, hard 5px 5px 0 #000 shadows, saturated flat fills (e.g. #FFD60A, #FF6B9D, #A3E635) on white, 0-4px radii, heavy grotesk headings; on press translate the element 5px down-right onto its shadow in 80ms with no easing softness.

options.what: Interface composed like magazine or editorial layout.
options.looks: Large serif or display headlines, strong typographic hierarchy, asymmetric grids, generous margins, pull quotes, image-led modules.
options.motion: Typographic motion: line-by-line reveals, masked text wipes, measured page-turn-like transitions.
options.use: Publishing and content tools, luxury and fashion commerce, brand-led product films.
options.conveys: Taste, authority, culture, considered craft.
options.vs: Minimal UI is sparse; editorial UI can be dense but typographically led. Bento UI uses equal cards; editorial uses an asymmetric grid with dominant type.
options.prompt: Compose the interface as an editorial spread: a large serif display headline (80-140px), a 12-column asymmetric grid with one dominant image module, small caps labels, thin rules between sections; reveal text line by line with masked upward wipes (500-700ms, power3.out, 60-80ms stagger).

options.what: Interface inspired by old operating systems, early websites or vintage hardware.
options.looks: Beveled gray windows, pixel fonts, title bars with close boxes, dithered icons, 16-color palettes, early-web tiled backgrounds; sub-styles include Mac OS classic, Windows 95, Y2K chrome, and early web.
options.motion: Stepped, low-framerate motion: windows pop in without easing, cursors jump, progress bars fill in blocks, CRT flicker.
options.use: Nostalgia campaigns, playful brands, music and culture content, parody.
options.conveys: Nostalgia, humor, internet culture.
options.vs: Terminal UI is specifically command-line; retro UI covers GUI eras. Era/visual-style dimensions define the broader period look; this defines how the interface itself is drawn.
options.prompt: Render the interface as a 1990s operating system: gray (#C0C0C0) windows with 2px bevel highlights and shadows, navy title bars, pixel or bitmap fonts, 1-bit or 16-color icons; animate with no easing, step-based moves at 12-15fps, block-filled progress bars and instant window pops.

options.what: Monospace, command-line or code-editor interfaces.
options.looks: Dark background, monospace type, syntax highlighting, prompt characters, blinking block cursor, line numbers, minimal chrome.
options.motion: Character-by-character typing, line-by-line output scroll, blinking cursor at ~530ms, spinners, instant command results.
options.use: Developer tools, APIs, infrastructure, AI agents, security products.
options.conveys: Technical competence, speed, power-user credibility.
options.vs: FUI invents fictional sci-fi data displays; terminal UI depicts real command-line conventions. Retro UI can include old terminals (green phosphor) but is about period, not function.
options.prompt: Render a terminal or code editor: near-black background (#0B0B0F), 16-20px monospace text, syntax colors from one theme, a '$' or '>' prompt; type commands at 25-45ms per character with slight rhythm variation, print output line by line (30-60ms per line), and blink a block cursor at 530ms intervals.

options.what: HUDs, floating data and sci-fi interface language designed for fiction rather than use.
options.looks: Thin cyan or amber line work, circular gauges, tick-mark scales, micro-typography labels, scan lines, data readouts, targeting brackets, often on black or overlaid on footage.
options.motion: Constant micro-motion: numbers flicker, rings rotate, lines trace, brackets lock on, glitch or scan reveals.
options.use: Film and game screens, AI and security products, tech keynotes, event openers.
options.conveys: Advanced technology, surveillance, intelligence, the future.
options.vs: Terminal UI is real developer tooling; FUI is invented and decorative. Spatial UI puts real panels in 3D; FUI is a graphic language. 'FUI' is established screen-graphics jargon.
options.prompt: Build a HUD-style interface: 0.5-1px cyan (#00E5FF) or amber line work on near-black, concentric rings with tick marks, 9-11px uppercase monospace labels, bracketed readouts; keep constant micro-motion (rings rotating at 5-20 deg/s, numbers flickering every 80-120ms, lines tracing on with linear eases) and reveal modules with scan-line wipes.

options.what: Interface panels floating and arranged in three-dimensional space.
options.looks: Multiple panels at different depths and angles, perspective, depth-of-field blur on distant panels, often glass surfaces.
options.motion: Camera orbits, dollies and parallax through the panel arrangement; panels rotate to face the camera or rearrange in depth.
options.use: Launch films, XR and visionOS products, showing an ecosystem or many features at once.
options.conveys: Scale, immersion, a whole platform.
options.vs: Deviceless UI floats but typically in 2D; spatial UI uses real z-depth and camera movement. Exploded UI separates one interface's layers; spatial UI arranges many panels.
options.prompt: Arrange 3-7 UI panels in 3D space at depths from z=-800 to z=200 with 5-25 degree Y rotations; use perspective 1200-2000px, blur distant panels 4-8px for depth of field, and move the camera with a slow orbit or dolly (4-6 s, sine.inOut) so panels parallax.

options.what: Interface shown inside a phone, laptop, tablet or watch.
options.looks: Realistic or simplified device frame (bezels, notch, Dynamic Island, keyboard) holding the screen; often a clean studio background.
options.motion: Device rotates, tilts or slides in; screen content scrolls or transitions inside; hands or taps may appear.
options.use: Mobile apps, app-store previews, cross-device stories, hardware-plus-software launches.
options.conveys: Tangibility and context: this runs on your device.
options.vs: Browser-framed UI uses browser chrome, not hardware. In-context UI places the device in a real environment; device-bound can be on a plain background.
options.prompt: Place the UI inside a device frame (e.g. a modern phone with 44-55px corner radius and thin bezels, or a laptop with hinge and keyboard); keep the frame neutral (graphite or silver) with soft studio reflection; animate the device entering with a 3D rotation of 10-20 degrees settling flat, then drive transitions inside the screen.

options.what: Interface floats independently with no physical device or window.
options.looks: Screens or panels as bare rounded rectangles over a background, usually with soft shadows.
options.motion: UI moves freely: scales, slides, rotates in 2D or 2.5D; transitions between screens are unconstrained by a frame.
options.use: SaaS launch films, feature reveals, web products, cross-platform products.
options.conveys: Modernity and platform independence; focus on software.
options.vs: Floating-card UI breaks the UI into several fragments; deviceless UI shows a whole screen without a frame. Full-screen UI fills the composition edge-to-edge.
options.prompt: Show the interface as a bare panel with no device or browser chrome: 12-20px radius, 1px subtle border, soft diffuse shadow, floating over a plain or gradient background at 70-85% of frame width; move it freely with 2.5D tilts under 15 degrees.

options.what: Product shown inside a browser window with tabs, address bar and traffic-light controls.
options.looks: Simplified browser chrome (three traffic-light dots, URL bar, maybe tabs) around the web app.
options.motion: URL types in, page loads, tabs switch; the window scales in or the camera pushes into the page.
options.use: Web apps, SaaS, websites and landing pages, extension products.
options.conveys: It is on the web; nothing to install.
options.vs: Windowed UI shows several OS windows; browser-framed shows one web product in browser chrome. Device-bound adds hardware.
options.prompt: Wrap the product in simplified browser chrome: a 40-48px top bar with three 12px traffic-light circles, a pill URL field showing the product domain, optional one or two tabs; keep chrome neutral and low contrast so the page reads first.

options.what: Multiple desktop or application windows shown together.
options.looks: Overlapping OS-style windows with title bars, possibly a desktop background and dock or taskbar.
options.motion: Windows open, close, stack, tile, and drag; focus shifts between windows; content passes from one app to another.
options.use: Desktop apps, integrations, workflows across tools, productivity software.
options.conveys: Multitasking, integration, real work context.
options.vs: Browser-framed shows one web app; windowed shows several apps or windows interacting. Retro UI can be windowed but in period style.
options.prompt: Show 2-4 application windows overlapping on a desktop: each with a 28-36px title bar, 10-12px radius, layered elevation shadow; animate windows opening from a 0.9 scale with 250-350ms ease-out, dragging with inertia, and passing content between them.

options.what: The product occupies the entire composition with no frame or background visible.
options.looks: The frame is the app: UI fills 100% of the canvas edge to edge.
options.motion: In-product navigation and camera push-ins or crops inside the interface; cuts between screens.
options.use: Demos, tutorials, screen-recording-style videos, app previews.
options.conveys: Immersion and directness: you are using it.
options.vs: Deviceless UI floats on a background; full-screen UI is the background. Screen recordings are usually full-screen but not necessarily recreated.
options.prompt: Fill the entire canvas with the interface, edge to edge, no background visible; create emphasis by animating a virtual camera within it (scale 1.0-2.0 push-ins, pans to regions in use) rather than by moving the UI as an object.

options.what: UI fragments separated into independent cards floating in the composition.
options.looks: Several cards (a stat, a chart, a notification, a profile) at varied sizes and positions, overlapping slightly, soft shadows.
options.motion: Cards drift and parallax, enter with staggered offsets, update values, and rearrange.
options.use: Hero sections, feature overviews, social ads, landing-page animations.
options.conveys: Breadth of capability, lightness, modularity.
options.vs: Bento UI arranges cards in a strict grid; floating-card UI scatters them freely. Deconstructed UI shows a whole screen breaking into pieces; floating-card starts from fragments.
options.prompt: Extract 3-6 UI fragments (stat card, mini chart, notification, avatar row) as independent cards with 16-20px radius and soft shadows; scatter them at varied scales (0.8-1.2) with slight overlaps and rotations under 6 degrees; stagger their entrances by 80-120ms and give each a slow idle drift of 4-10px.

options.what: Interface shown on devices within a real or rendered environment (desk, hand, room).
options.looks: Photographic or 3D-rendered scenes: a laptop on a desk, a phone in hand, a screen in a store; UI composited onto the screen.
options.motion: Camera moves through the environment; screen content is tracked onto the device; cuts between people and screens.
options.use: Brand films, consumer products, showing who uses the product and where.
options.conveys: Real-world relevance and human context.
options.vs: Device-bound UI usually sits on a clean background; in-context UI lives in a scene with people and places.
options.prompt: Place the UI on a device inside a realistic environment (photo or 3D render): match screen perspective with corner-pin tracking, add a subtle glass reflection at 5-10% and match the scene's color temperature; keep UI content large and simple enough to read at the device's scale in frame.

options.what: A flat screen rotated in 3D perspective so it lies at an angle, often receding into space.
options.looks: A screen tilted 15-45 degrees on X and/or Y, sometimes lying almost flat like a table, with foreshortening and a long soft shadow.
options.motion: Screens rotate from tilted to flat-on (or vice versa) to transition between overview and detail; camera slides along the tilted surface.
options.use: Launch film openers, landing heroes, showing large interfaces dramatically.
options.conveys: Drama and depth while keeping software recognisable.
options.vs: Spatial UI arranges many panels in 3D; perspective-tilted UI rotates one flat screen. Isometric UI uses parallel projection (no vanishing point).
options.prompt: Rotate the flat UI in 3D: rotateX 20-40 degrees and rotateZ -10 to -20 degrees with perspective 1500-2500px, a long soft shadow beneath; transition by animating to flat-on (rotateX 0, rotateZ 0) over 1-1.4 s with power3.inOut as the camera pushes in.

options.what: Interface drawn in isometric (parallel) projection, typically at 30-degree axes with no vanishing point.
options.looks: Screens and cards as tilted slabs with visible thickness, stacked layers, all parallel lines; diagram-like.
options.motion: Layers lift vertically along the z-axis, blocks slide along isometric axes, stacks build up.
options.use: Architecture and platform explainers, infrastructure products, layered-system diagrams.
options.conveys: System thinking, structure, a whole platform in one view.
options.vs: Perspective-tilted UI has a vanishing point; isometric has none. Exploded UI often uses isometric projection to show layers, but exploded is the construction move and isometric the projection.
options.prompt: Render the interface in true isometric projection (rotateX 54.7 deg, rotateZ -45 deg, orthographic, no perspective), give cards 4-8px visible thickness; animate layers lifting along the vertical axis in 20-40px steps with 60-100ms stagger.

options.what: Interface layers pulled apart along the depth axis to show how they stack.
options.looks: The same screen split into parallel planes (background, content, controls, overlays) separated in z, like a technical exploded-view drawing.
options.motion: Layers separate from a flat composite in z, the camera orbits to reveal the stack, then layers recompose.
options.use: Explaining architecture, design systems, what powers a screen; hero moments in launch films.
options.conveys: Depth, craft, what is under the surface.
options.vs: Deconstructed UI breaks a screen into its components scattered in plane; exploded UI keeps the components aligned but separates layers in depth. The term comes from engineering exploded-view drawings.
options.prompt: Start with the flat composed screen, then separate it into 3-6 layers (background, containers, content, controls, overlays) along z with 80-200px gaps while rotating the whole stack to 40-60 degrees X and -30 degrees Z; use 1.2-1.6 s power3.inOut, hold, then collapse back.

options.what: A normal interface breaks into its constituent pieces, which scatter or rearrange.
options.looks: Buttons, cards, text blocks and icons pulled out of the layout and floating apart in the same plane or loosely in space.
options.motion: The screen shatters or unzips into components, which drift, reorder, then reassemble into a new layout or state.
options.use: Transitions between features, design-system launches, showing modularity.
options.conveys: Modularity and flexibility; the product is made of parts you can rearrange.
options.vs: Exploded UI keeps layers aligned and separates them in depth; deconstructed UI lets pieces leave their positions. Floating-card UI starts fragmented; deconstructed shows the breaking.
options.prompt: Begin with a complete screen, then pull its 8-15 components out of the layout: each travels 100-400px in its own direction with slight rotation (under 10 degrees), staggered 30-50ms; after a hold, reassemble them into a new arrangement with 800ms power3.inOut.

options.what: Only one button, field, card or control is shown.
options.looks: A single component centered on a plain background, at true or enlarged scale, with its full state detail visible.
options.motion: Micro-interaction studies: hover, press, loading, success, each state change animated precisely.
options.use: Design-system showcases, micro-interaction reels, feature teasers, social loops.
options.conveys: Care and precision in every detail.
options.vs: Abstracted UI keeps a few related components; isolated-component shows exactly one. Oversized UI blows it up as a graphic element.
options.prompt: Show exactly one component (e.g. a button or input) centered on a plain background at 2-3x true scale; animate its full state sequence (idle, hover, press, loading, success) with precise timings: 120ms hover, 80ms press, loading spinner, 300ms success morph.

options.what: Small UI components become enormous graphic elements dominating the frame.
options.looks: A toggle, cursor, checkbox or button filling most of the frame, often cropped by the edges, used like a supergraphic.
options.motion: Weighty, physical motion: the giant toggle slides like a heavy object, the cursor sweeps across the frame; camera may push through elements.
options.use: Ads, social openers, typographic launch films, poster-like moments.
options.conveys: Boldness and impact; a single action becomes monumental.
options.vs: Isolated-component UI shows one component at readable scale; oversized UI blows it up beyond the frame as graphic form. Micro-UI is the opposite scale.
options.prompt: Scale one UI element (toggle, cursor, checkbox, button) until it fills 60-120% of the frame, letting edges crop it; keep exact proportions, radius and stroke ratios; animate with weight (longer 600-900ms moves, power4.out) as if it were a large physical object.

options.what: Tiny controls, badges and interface fragments used as visual elements, texture or punctuation.
options.looks: Small chips, pills, toggles, avatars and status dots scattered around type or imagery, or tiled as patterns.
options.motion: Quick pops, ticks and flips; many small elements animating in rhythm or as a field.
options.use: Brand systems, typographic pieces, background textures, social content.
options.conveys: Digital nativeness, busyness, a living ecosystem.
options.vs: Isolated-component UI makes one control the subject; micro-UI uses many tiny controls as supporting graphics. Decorative role facet is related.
options.prompt: Use tiny UI elements (toggles 24-32px wide, pills, status dots, avatar chips) as graphic punctuation around the hero content: 10-30 elements, each animating a quick state flip (80-150ms) on a staggered rhythm of 100-200ms; keep them below the hero in contrast.

options.what: Information presented through modular cards of varied size packed into a strict grid.
options.looks: Rounded rectangles of 1x1, 2x1, 2x2 spans tightly packed with equal 12-24px gutters, each card holding one feature, stat or visual.
options.motion: Cards reveal in a staggered cascade, individual cards play their own small loops, and a card may expand to fill the grid.
options.use: Feature overviews, landing pages, keynote spec summaries, year-in-review.
options.conveys: Breadth at a glance, organisation, completeness.
options.vs: Dashboard UI shows live operational data; bento is a presentation layout. Floating-card UI is free-scattered; bento is gridded with equal gutters. The name comes from Japanese bento boxes; popularised by Apple keynote slides.
options.prompt: Arrange 6-9 cards in a bento grid on a 4-column base: mixed 1x1, 2x1 and 2x2 spans, 16px gutters, 20-24px radius; each card holds one idea (icon plus short label, a stat, a mini visual); reveal with a diagonal stagger of 50-70ms (scale 0.96 to 1, opacity 0 to 1, 500ms power3.out).

options.what: Charts, tables, KPI cards and metrics composed into an operational overview.
options.looks: Sidebar navigation, KPI tiles with big numbers, line and bar charts, data tables, filters, status badges.
options.motion: Numbers count up, charts draw on, rows populate with stagger, filters change and data morphs.
options.use: Analytics, fintech, B2B SaaS, monitoring and observability.
options.conveys: Control, insight, data-driven confidence.
options.vs: Bento UI is a presentation grid; dashboard UI is working data. Data-viz (separate dimension) defines how the charts animate; this defines the interface around them.
options.prompt: Build a dashboard: left sidebar, a row of 3-4 KPI tiles with large tabular-figure numbers, one main line or area chart, a secondary bar chart and a short table; animate numbers counting up over 800-1200ms (power2.out), chart lines drawing on left to right, and table rows entering with 40ms stagger.

options.what: Conversation and message bubbles dominate the interface.
options.looks: Alternating message bubbles or AI response blocks, avatars, input bar at the bottom, typing indicator.
options.motion: Bubbles pop in from their sender side, typing indicators pulse, AI responses stream in token by token, the thread scrolls up.
options.use: AI assistants, messaging and support products, social apps, conversational explainers.
options.conveys: Conversation, responsiveness, human or AI presence.
options.vs: Command-palette UI is one-shot search and action; chat UI is a turn-by-turn thread. Terminal UI is also text-in/text-out but monospace and command-based.
options.prompt: Show a conversation thread: user bubbles right-aligned in the accent color, responses left-aligned on a neutral surface, 18-20px radius with a tighter corner at the tail side; each bubble enters with 250ms scale from 0.9 at its origin corner; AI replies stream in 2-4 words at a time after a 3-dot typing indicator.

options.what: A search and command interface as the hero object.
options.looks: A centered floating input with a result list beneath: icons, labels, keyboard shortcut hints, highlighted selected row, dimmed backdrop.
options.motion: Palette scales in from 0.96 with backdrop dim, query types in, results filter and reorder live, selection bar slides between rows, Enter triggers the action.
options.use: Productivity tools, developer tools, launchers, keyboard-first products.
options.conveys: Speed, keyboard mastery, everything one keystroke away.
options.vs: Search UI is broader (pages, results); command palette combines search with actions and shortcuts in an overlay. Chat UI is conversational and persistent.
options.prompt: Show a centered command palette 560-680px wide: search input on top, 6-8 result rows with icons, labels and right-aligned shortcut keycaps; enter with scale 0.96 to 1 and opacity over 160ms while the backdrop dims to 40%; type the query at 40-60ms per character, filter results live, and slide the highlight bar between rows in 100ms.

options.what: Inputs, toggles, selectors and controls dominate the interface.
options.looks: Labeled fields, dropdowns, toggles, checkboxes, segmented controls and a primary button, in vertical rhythm.
options.motion: Fields focus in sequence, values type in, toggles flip, validation checks appear, the submit button transitions to loading then success.
options.use: Onboarding, checkout, configuration and setup stories, no-code tools.
options.conveys: Ease and control: setup is quick and painless.
options.vs: Isolated-component UI shows one control; form-based UI shows a sequence of controls working together.
options.prompt: Build a vertical form of 3-6 fields with labels above inputs, toggles and one primary button; animate a focused completion sequence: focus ring appears (120ms), text types in, a green check validates each field (200ms), then the button morphs into a spinner and resolves to a success state.

options.what: An open canvas with objects, frames or connected nodes rather than a fixed page layout.
options.looks: Dotted-grid background, frames or nodes with ports, connecting bezier lines, toolbars floating at edges, multiplayer cursors.
options.motion: Canvas pans and zooms, nodes are dragged and connected with animated lines, data pulses along connectors.
options.use: Design tools, whiteboards, automation and workflow builders, AI agent builders.
options.conveys: Creative freedom, systems thinking, collaboration.
options.vs: Dashboard UI is a fixed grid of widgets; canvas UI is spatial and user-arranged. Workflow visualization (product-demo) is a demo approach; this is the interface type.
options.prompt: Show an infinite canvas: a 16-24px dotted grid background, 3-6 nodes or frames with rounded corners and ports, bezier connectors 1.5-2px; pan and zoom the canvas with smooth 600-900ms moves, drag a new node in, draw its connector on, and send a small dot pulse along the connection.

options.what: Small glanceable surfaces: notifications, widgets, live activities, menu-bar popovers.
options.looks: Compact rounded cards with an app icon, one line of title, one of detail, maybe a mini progress or chart.
options.motion: Banners slide down from the top, widgets update values in place, stacks expand and collapse.
options.use: Mobile features, alerts and monitoring products, ambient updates, social ads.
options.conveys: Immediacy and presence in the user's day.
options.vs: Floating-card UI uses fragments of a full app; widget UI shows OS-level glanceable surfaces. Toast and notification in ui-interaction define the motion.
options.prompt: Show compact glanceable cards (width 340-380px, 20-24px radius, app icon plus title and one detail line); slide notifications down from the top edge with a 350ms spring-like ease, stack subsequent ones with 8px offsets and 0.95 scale behind, and update widget values in place with a rolling number.

options.what: Interface that resembles software but exists mainly to communicate an idea, not a real product.
options.looks: Plausible-looking controls with exaggerated or impossible behavior: a slider labeled 'chaos to calm', a progress bar for 'trust', a search bar containing a big idea.
options.motion: UI behaves symbolically: controls change the world around them, not just data.
options.use: Brand films, manifestos, ads, conceptual explainers, early products without real UI.
options.conveys: Wit and concept; the idea is instantly legible through familiar UI grammar.
options.vs: Stylized UI is based on the real product; faux UI represents no real product. Illustrative UI is a drawing style; faux UI is a rhetorical device and can use any style.
options.prompt: Use familiar UI grammar to express an idea rather than a product: invent a control whose label is the concept (e.g. a slider from 'busy' to 'focused', a toggle labeled 'noise'), style it cleanly and plausibly, and let operating it transform the scene around it.
